notes: App-level verification catalog. The additive fields (when/owner/proves/onFail/evidence/estMinutes) turn a catalog entry into a cutover gate: `when` says whether it must pass BEFORE traffic moves, AFTER, or only inside a recovery test; `onFail` says whether a failure stops the cutover or is advisory. An entry with no `when` is recovery-test-only, which is how every pre-existing workspace behaves. Owners here are ROLES — replace them with the person who actually said they would run it.

templates.name: Claim submitted returns a business response (not a 500)
templates.expected: HTTP 200 with a real claim_id / adjudication result in the body — an error page or internal_server_error is a FAIL even if the pod is green
templates.hint: This is the front half of the success bar. Use the partner-shaped payload, not a health check.
templates.proves: A customer-visible transaction completes end to end in the recovery region
templates.evidence: Paste the claim_id and the full response body into the bridge log

templates.name: Settlement/remittance import runs end-to-end
templates.command: kubectl -n <ns> create job --from=cronjob/<settlement-import> dr-test-import && kubectl logs -f job/dr-test-import
templates.expected: Import completes; new rows visible in the recovered remittance database
templates.hint: The back half of the success bar. Batch paths fail differently from request paths — test both.
templates.proves: The batch path — not just the request path — works against recovered data
templates.evidence: Job name, exit status, and the row count before/after

templates.name: Auth flow works against recovered identity provider
templates.expected: Valid token issued and accepted by a protected endpoint
templates.hint: Identity pools / authorizers are region-bound more often than teams expect.
templates.proves: Callers can still authenticate once traffic arrives in the recovery region
templates.evidence: Token issued at <time>, accepted by <protected endpoint>

templates.name: Async queue consumers drain a test message
templates.command: aws sqs send-message --queue-url <recovered-queue-url> --message-body @test-message.json && watch queue depth
templates.expected: Message consumed within normal latency; downstream side effect observed
templates.hint: Consumers that started before the queue existed may be wedged — check consumer age vs queue age.
templates.proves: The asynchronous half of the system is alive, not just the synchronous half
templates.evidence: Message id, time consumed, the downstream record it produced

templates.name: Database freshness query (measures RPA)
templates.expected: Age at T0 within the recovery-point window — record the number as measured RPA
templates.hint: Run against every Tier-0 database; the worst number is the honest RPA.
templates.proves: How much data the business is about to lose, as a number, before anyone approves losing it
templates.evidence: The literal interval per Tier-0 store, and which store was worst

templates.name: Write path lands in the recovery region (writer endpoint check)
templates.command: psql -h <recovered-db> -c "SELECT inet_server_addr(), current_setting('cluster_name'); INSERT INTO <canary-table> VALUES (now()) RETURNING *;"
templates.expected: The write succeeds against a writer in the RECOVERY region — not a read-only replica, and not a writer still in the primary region
templates.hint: A promotion that half-happened reads fine and writes nowhere. Prove a write, not a SELECT 1.
templates.proves: The data primary really moved, so accepting traffic will not fail on the first write
templates.evidence: Writer endpoint/region and the returned canary row

templates.name: Old primary is fenced — no writer still accepting writes
templates.command: From the primary region (if reachable): attempt a write against the old writer endpoint; confirm it is rejected/demoted
templates.expected: The old writer refuses writes (or is unreachable). Two writers is split-brain, and split-brain is not recoverable by a runbook.
templates.hint: Fence BEFORE promote, verify fencing BEFORE cutover. Ungraceful ARC failover does NOT demote the old writer for you.
templates.proves: There is exactly one place writes can land when traffic moves
templates.evidence: The rejection message, or evidence the primary is unreachable

templates.name: Secrets resolution clean (secrets-init or equivalent)
templates.expected: Zero resolution errors; every logical name resolves in the recovery region
templates.hint: The most common test-killer. Check BEFORE blaming the app.
templates.proves: The applications can obtain the credentials they need with the primary region dark
templates.evidence: Clean log excerpt per Tier-0 workload

templates.name: Images pulled from recovery-region registry
templates.expected: Every image host is the recovery-region registry — zero references to the primary region
templates.hint: A pod pulling cross-region from the 'dead' primary passes the test and fails the disaster.
templates.proves: The stack survives the primary region going away, rather than quietly depending on it

templates.name: Edge reachable via direct endpoint + Host header (no DNS change)
templates.expected: HTTP 200 from recovered backends through the recovered edge chain
templates.hint: Proves L5 without touching public DNS — the Phase-1 way to test the front door.
templates.proves: The front door answers before any public DNS is changed, so the cutover is reversible right up to the flip
templates.evidence: Status code and the certificate CN/SAN seen on the connection

templates.name: Outbound third-party call succeeds from recovery egress
templates.command: From a recovered pod: curl -s <partner-api-endpoint>/ping (or the app's own outbound health probe)
templates.expected: Partner endpoint answers — proves egress routing, NAT, and any partner allowlist
templates.hint: If the partner allowlists source IPs, this fails until recovery egress IPs are registered.
templates.proves: The one thing that cannot be fixed during the event — a partner allowlist — is already correct
templates.evidence: Partner response and the source IP it saw

templates.name: Partner webhook received by recovered stack
templates.command: Ask partner (or webhook simulator) to POST to the direct recovery endpoint
templates.expected: Webhook accepted, signature verified, downstream processing observed
templates.hint: Inbound partner traffic exercises authorizers and allowlists that outbound tests miss.
templates.proves: Inbound partner traffic is accepted, not only outbound partner traffic
templates.evidence: Webhook id and the processing record it produced

templates.name: Cache rebuild path works cold
templates.command: redis-cli -h <recovered-redis> dbsize; then exercise an app path that populates it
templates.expected: App serves correctly (if slower) with a cold cache; cache fills as traffic flows
templates.hint: Caches are usually rebuilt, not restored — prove the app tolerates empty.
templates.proves: An empty cache is a latency problem, not an outage, when live traffic lands
templates.evidence: dbsize before/after and the observed latency

templates.name: Observability shows the recovery stack
templates.command: Open the DR dashboard; confirm metrics/logs flowing from recovery-region workloads
templates.expected: Dashboards populated with live recovery-region data — the runbook gates are readable
templates.hint: If you can't see it, you can't verify it; a blind recovery passes on vibes.
templates.proves: The people on the bridge can see what happens after the flip
templates.evidence: Dashboard link and the last data point timestamp

templates.name: Scheduled report/batch job generates output
templates.expected: Report written to the recovered bucket with today's date
templates.hint: Report jobs find region-bound bucket names and stale IAM faster than anything else.
templates.proves: The reporting tail of the system survived the move — it can be fixed after traffic is safe
templates.evidence: Object key and size in the recovered bucket

templates.name: First LIVE partner transaction after the flip
templates.command: Ask the partner to send one real transaction against the public domain (not the direct endpoint)
templates.expected: The transaction is accepted and adjudicated end to end over the public path
templates.hint: The direct-endpoint test proves the stack; this proves DNS, TLS, WAF and the partner's own routing.
templates.proves: Live customer traffic really is being served from the recovery region
templates.evidence: Partner reference and the transaction id on our side

templates.name: Error rate and latency on live traffic hold for one soak window
templates.command: Watch 5xx rate, p99 latency and queue depth for <soak-window> minutes after the flip
templates.expected: Error rate and latency within the agreed soak thresholds — a rising queue depth means consumers did not scale
templates.hint: The flip is not the end of the event. Decide the rollback trigger BEFORE the soak starts.
templates.proves: The recovery region holds real load, not just a single test transaction
templates.evidence: Dashboard screenshot at the end of the soak window

templates.name: Public DNS / routing state resolves to the recovery region everywhere
templates.command: dig +short api.<your-domain> from several resolvers; confirm the routing-control or health-check state
templates.expected: Resolvers return the recovery-region target; the routing control reads as expected in both regions
templates.hint: TTL and resolver caching mean 'flipped' and 'flipped everywhere' are different times.
templates.proves: The traffic move actually reached the public internet, not just the control plane
templates.evidence: Resolver answers and the time each one converged
